title: Elements, compounds and mixtures
learningObjective: Understand how to classify a substance as an element, compound or mixture; Understand how a chromatogram provides information about the composition of a mixture; Understand that a pure substance has a fixed melting and boiling point, but that a mixture may melt or boil over a range of temperatures; Describe these experimental techniques for the separation of mixtures: simple distillation; fractional distillation; filtration; crystallisation; paper chromatography; Understand how to use the calculation of Rf values to identify the components of a mixture; Practical: Investigate paper chromatography using inks/food colourings

sections.title: The map of all matter
sections.markdown:
Look around: nearly everything you meet in everyday life is a **mixture**.
The air you breathe contains elements such as nitrogen and oxygen along
with compounds such as carbon dioxide and nitrogen oxides. The food you eat
and the drinks you drink are mixtures too. Even a gold ring is not pure gold —
an 18-carat ring is only 75% gold, with the rest usually copper. Only a few
things — a nugget of pure metal, a diamond, a bottle of distilled water — come
close to being the single, uncontaminated substances chemists call **pure**.

Chemistry sorts every substance into one of three boxes: an [[element]], a
[[compound]] or a [[mixture]]. Getting that classification right is the
business of this lesson, and it matters far beyond the classroom. Most
forensic work starts by **separating** a mixture into its components — you
cannot analyse a sample until the things mixed into it are apart. By the end
of this lesson you will be able to:

- classify any substance as an element, compound or mixture;
- say why a pure substance melts and boils at a **fixed temperature** while a
  mixture melts and boils over a **range**;
- describe the four separation techniques — simple distillation, fractional
  distillation, filtration and crystallisation — plus paper chromatography;
- use a **chromatogram** and **Rf values** to work out what a mixture
  contains.

:::key-point
Every substance is an element, a compound or a mixture. Elements and
compounds are **pure**; mixtures are not, and their components can be
separated by physical means such as filtration or distillation.
:::

:::prior-knowledge
From Lesson u1:c01 (States of matter) you already know the terms **melting
point**, **boiling point**, **solute** and **solvent** — we use all of them
here, especially in the purity test (§s07) and the separation methods (§s09).
From Key Stage 3 you should remember that everything is made of atoms; if
the word *atom* is hazy for you, the book flags Chapter 3 as the place it is
properly defined.
:::

:::cross-curricular
**Forensics:** identifying an unknown substance — ink from a ransom letter,
a powder at a crime scene — always begins by separating the mixture and ends
with chromatography (§s10).
**Geography/industry:** producing fresh water from salt water (desalination)
is the simple distillation of §s09 at industrial scale.
:::

:::misconception
"The water we drink is pure water." No — pure water is a compound (H₂O
only). Drinking water is a **mixture**: water with dissolved substances in
it. That is exactly why it boils over a range, not at exactly 100 °C.
:::

:::exam-hint
"Classify" and "state whether … is an element, compound or mixture" are
1-mark command words: give the box, then (for 2 marks) the reason — e.g.
"*mixture* because the components are not chemically joined and are present
in no fixed proportion". Reasons score; vibes do not.
:::

sections.title: Elements — one type of atom
sections.markdown:
An **[[element]]** is a substance that cannot be split into anything simpler
by chemical means. Every element contains only one kind of atom — heat it,
react it, electrocute it, and you will never chemically prize an element
apart into different substances. In models and diagrams, elements are drawn
as atoms of a single colour or size. The book's examples are a pure metal
such as magnesium, oxygen gas, and diamond (a form of carbon) — three very
different materials, but each contains just one type of atom (Figure 2.3).

One subtlety, which the book flags in its margin: it is not *completely*
true to say an element contains only one type of atom. Most elements are
natural mixtures of **[[isotope]]s** — atoms with the same atomic number but
different mass numbers, because they carry different numbers of neutrons.
The precise statement is that all the atoms in an element have the same
**[[atomic-number]]**. Diagrams and models usually ignore the
difference between isotopes; they get their full treatment in Chapter 3.

:::key-point
The safe definition: all the atoms in an element have the **same atomic
number**. "Only one type of atom" is almost right, but isotopes mean most
elements contain atoms of slightly different masses — same protons,
different neutrons (Chapter 3).
:::

:::misconception
"Oxygen gas can't be an element — its particles contain two atoms joined
together." No — an element is defined by having **one type of atom**, not
one atom per particle. Oxygen gas contains only oxygen atoms, so it is an
element; the same is true of nitrogen, hydrogen and chlorine gases.
:::

:::exam-hint
"State what is meant by an *element*" (1 mark): mark schemes accept
"a substance that cannot be broken down into anything simpler by chemical
means" or "contains only one type of atom / atoms with the same atomic
number". Avoid circular answers like "an element is a substance made of
elements".
:::

sections.title: 118 elements — and where they live
sections.markdown:
So how many elements are there? **118**, and every single one of them lives
on the **[[periodic-table]]** — the chart that hangs on every chemistry
laboratory wall. Most of them occur naturally on Earth: hydrogen, helium
and sulfur are everyday examples you will meet throughout this course. A
few do not occur naturally at all and have to be made artificially, in
particle accelerators and nuclear reactors; einsteinium is one of these.

For this lesson the count itself is not the point — the point is that the
periodic table is the *complete catalogue* of elements. Every substance
that is not on it is either a compound built from two or more of its
entries (§s04) or a mixture of such substances (§s05).

:::key-point
There are 118 elements, all displayed in the periodic table. Most occur
naturally (hydrogen, helium, sulfur); a handful are made artificially
(einsteinium).
:::

:::misconception
"Artificial elements are not real chemicals." No — an element is defined
by its atoms (same atomic number), not by where it came from. Einsteinium
is as much an element as hydrogen; it is simply one humans have to
manufacture because it does not occur naturally.
:::

:::exam-hint
"State the number of elements shown in the periodic table" or "give the
name of an element that occurs naturally" (1 mark): **118**; any natural
element named from the periodic table. Keep it short — command word
"state" wants one line.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join (derived-links law): spec 1.8 × 2 items — how many
elements exist; natural vs artificial elements. Book p. 15 → page jump.
:::

sections.title: Compounds — elements in fixed proportions
sections.markdown:
A **[[compound]]** is formed when two or more elements **chemically
combine** — and the moment that reaction happens, the proportions lock. The
elements always combine in **fixed proportions**: the same compound, made
in London or on Mars, always contains exactly the same ratio of its
elements. Hydrogen and fluorine always combine to form hydrogen fluoride,
[[formula]] HF; magnesium and fluorine always form magnesium fluoride,
MgF₂; carbon dioxide is always CO₂ and methane always CH₄. You cannot make
a "stronger" or "weaker" carbon dioxide by using more carbon or more oxygen
— chemistry does not negotiate on ratios.

In diagrams, a compound shows **more than one type of atom bonded
together** (Figure 2.4). That picture is worth pausing on: the atoms are
not just mixed side by side as in a mixture — they are *bonded*, which is
precisely why undoing a compound needs a chemical reaction (§s06).

:::key-point
Compounds = two or more elements chemically combined in **fixed
proportions**. Hydrogen fluoride is always HF; magnesium fluoride is always
MgF₂; carbon dioxide is always CO₂. Diagrams show two or more atom types
bonded together.
:::

:::misconception
"You can make carbon dioxide with different proportions of carbon and
oxygen, like mixing more or less squash in water." No — that is mixture
thinking. In a compound the ratio is fixed by the bonding: CO₂ is always
two oxygen atoms per carbon atom, never more, never fewer. Change the
ratio and you are either making a different compound or leaving unreacted
excess behind.
:::

:::exam-hint
"Explain why magnesium oxide is a compound" (2 marks): mark schemes want
both halves — (i) it contains two (or more) elements **chemically
combined**, and (ii) the elements are present in **fixed proportion**.
Writing only "it has different types of atom" describes a mixture of atoms
just as well — the "chemically combined" phrase is what scores.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join (derived-links law): spec 1.8 × 3 items — identify the
compound from particle diagrams; explain fixed proportions; distinguish
compound vs mixture from a description. Book Figure 2.4 → page jump to
book p. 15.
:::

sections.title: Mixtures — anything goes
sections.markdown:
A **[[mixture]]** is what you get when substances are simply put together —
**no chemical reaction occurs**. The components can be elements, compounds,
or both at once, and (unlike a compound) they can be present in **any
proportion**: you can put in as much or as little of each component as you
like, and it is still the same mixture. Nothing locks the ratio in, because
nothing has reacted.

The book's Figure 2.5 gives the three possible recipes, and they are worth
memorising as a classification toolkit:

- a **mixture of elements** — nitrogen and oxygen (this is essentially the
  air);
- a **mixture of compounds** — carbon dioxide and water vapour;
- a **mixture of an element with a compound** — carbon dioxide and nitrogen.

Because no reaction happens, the components keep their own properties and
can be got back apart by physical means — the theme of §s06 and §s09.

:::key-point
In a mixture no chemical reaction occurs; the components (elements
and/or compounds) can be present in **any proportion**. Mixtures of
elements, of compounds, and of an element with a compound are all possible.
:::

:::misconception
"A mixture has to be made of either all elements or all compounds." No —
the third combination is just as legal: an element mixed with a compound
(carbon dioxide and nitrogen, Figure 2.5). Classification asks *what is in
it and has it reacted*, not which single category the contents belong to.
:::

:::exam-hint
2-mark "explain why X is a mixture" answers score with: (i) the substances
are **not chemically joined** (no reaction has occurred) and (ii) they are
**not in fixed proportions** / can be mixed in any ratio. Either half alone
usually banks 1 mark; both halves bank both.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join (derived-links law): spec 1.8 × 3 items — classify the
three Figure 2.5 recipes; mixture vs compound from proportion statements;
spot the mixture from a diagram of different atoms not bonded. Book
Figure 2.5 → page jump to book p. 15.
:::

sections.title: Mixture or compound — the simple differences
sections.markdown:
Water is the book's cleanest contrast. In **water** (a compound), every
single water molecule has two hydrogen atoms combined with one oxygen atom
— it never varies. In a **mixture of hydrogen and oxygen gases**, the two
can be present in any proportion you fancy. The same story with iron and
sulfur: as a mixture you can combine them in any ratio, but iron sulfide
(FeS) — the compound — always contains iron and sulfur in exactly the same
proportion.

Proportions are only half the story. The other half is **properties**. In a
mixture of iron and sulfur, each element keeps its own properties: the iron
stays grey, the sulfur stays yellow, and when you add dilute hydrochloric
acid the iron fizzes to produce hydrogen while the sulfur does not react at
all. The compound iron sulfide behaves completely differently — it reacts
with acids in its own way, unlike either element. Compare a mixture of
hydrogen and oxygen with the compound water: put a flame to the mixture and
it explodes; the compound, water, is a colourless liquid that simply puts
the flame out.

**Separation follows the same divide.** Mixtures can be separated by
**physical means** — methods like changing the temperature or dissolving
part of the mixture, which involve no chemical reactions. A magnet pulls
the iron out of an iron–sulfur mixture while the sulfur stays behind. The
elements in a compound, though, cannot be separated by physical means:
turning water back into hydrogen and oxygen requires electrolysis (a
chemical process — Chapter 10). You *can* separate a mixture of hydrogen
and oxygen physically, though — oxygen condenses to a liquid at a much
higher temperature than hydrogen (−183 °C as opposed to −253 °C), so
cooling far enough leaves the oxygen liquid while hydrogen stays gaseous.

Finally, the vocabulary of purity: a mixture is not a pure substance. If a
sample contains only a small amount of an unwanted substance, that
unwanted substance is called an **[[impurity]]**.

:::key-point
Mixture: components in **any proportion**, each **keeping its own
properties**, separable by **physical means**. Compound: **fixed
proportion**, its **own new properties**, separable only by **chemical
reactions** (e.g. electrolysis of water).
:::

:::misconception
"Iron sulfide is just iron and sulfur sitting next to each other, so it
still reacts with acid like iron does." No — once iron and sulfur are
chemically combined, the individual properties are gone. Iron sulfide
reacts with acids differently from iron; sulfur's reaction with the acid
disappears too. New bonds mean new substance.
:::

:::exam-hint
The 4–6 mark "compare a mixture of iron and sulfur with the compound iron
sulfide" answer earns marks per difference stated: composition (any ratio
vs fixed), properties (kept vs new — use the acid test), separation
(physical vs chemical). Mark schemes reward precise comparisons, so write
"the **mixture** keeps the properties of iron and sulfur" — not just
"they are different".
:::

sections.title: Melting and boiling points — the purity test
sections.markdown:
Pure substances — elements and pure compounds alike — melt and boil at
**fixed temperatures**. Water melts at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C; every
clean sample of water does exactly the same. **Mixtures usually melt and
boil over a range of temperatures** instead. That single contrast is spec
point 1.9, and it hands you a practical purity test.

Impurities push both numbers the "wrong" way: they **lower the melting
point** and **raise the boiling point**. Dissolve 10 g of common salt
(sodium chloride) in 1 litre of water and the melting point drops to about
−0.6 °C while the boiling point climbs to about 100.2 °C. (This is why salt
gritters scatter salt on winter roads — the salty water is harder to freeze
than pure water.)

The melting point gives chemists a working purity test. Suppose you make
aspirin in a sixth-form practical. Aspirin is a white powder that melts at
138 °C. You record the temperature at which your sample *starts* to melt
and the temperature at which it has *fully* melted. If your sample melts
anywhere in the range 128–134 °C you know it is quite impure — it melts
over a wide range, and below the melting point of the pure substance.

Note how this reuses Lesson u1:c01: melting point and boiling point are the
same numbers you used to predict the state of a substance — but here they
become evidence about **what is dissolved in it**.

:::key-point
Pure substance → **fixed** melting and boiling point. Mixture → melts and
boils over a **range**. Impurities **lower** the melting point and
**raise** the boiling point. Melting point is the classic lab test for
purity.
:::

:::maths-skills
Reading a purity test is comparison logic, not calculation: (i) does the
sample melt at a single temperature or across a range? (ii) is that range
below the pure substance's melting point? Sample at 128–134 °C vs pure at
138 °C fails both tests at once — range *and* depression — so the verdict
is "impure" with two pieces of evidence.
:::

:::misconception
"Impurities raise the melting point, because there is more stuff to melt."
No — the opposite: dissolving an impurity **lowers** the melting point
(salt water freezes at about −0.6 °C, not above 0 °C) and raises the
boiling point (about 100.2 °C, not below 100 °C).
:::

:::exam-hint
"Substance X melts at 122 °C; substance Y melts between 87 and 93 °C.
Explain which is the pure substance" (2–3 marks): name **X**, then give the
reason in mark-scheme language — a pure substance has a **fixed/sharp
melting point**, while Y melts **over a range of temperatures**, so Y
contains an impurity. Both halves are needed: the verdict *and* the
fixed-vs-range rule.
:::

:::quick-check

verdict from melting data; effect of impurity on mp/bp; salt-water boiling
point. Book p. 16 → page jump.
:::

sections.title: Separation of mixtures — why and how
sections.markdown:
Separating mixtures is not a school-only exercise — it is one of the
load-bearing walls of the whole chemical industry. Crude oil arriving from
a well is a mixture of hundreds of hydrocarbons and is split by
distillation before anything useful can be made from it. Fresh water is
produced from salt water by distillation on an industrial scale. The
enrichment of uranium — separating two forms of the same element — is a
separation problem. And in forensic science, the components of a mixture
usually have to be **separated before they can be analysed**: an unseparated
sample tells you almost nothing.

The common thread: because mixtures were made by mixing (no reaction),
they can be undone by **physical means**. Which physical method you choose
depends on what is mixed with what — an insoluble solid in a liquid needs
**filtration** (Figure 2.6: sand from water), a dissolved solid needs
**crystallisation** or **simple distillation**, two miscible liquids need
**fractional distillation**, and dissolved dyes yield to **paper
chromatography**. Spec point 1.10 asks you to *describe* each of the first
four techniques; §s09 builds every one of them, and chromatography follows
in §s10.

:::key-point
Mixtures are separated by **physical means** because no chemical reaction
holds them together. The method is chosen by *what is mixed with what*:
insoluble solid → filtration; dissolved solid → crystallisation or simple
distillation; miscible liquids → fractional distillation; dyes → paper
chromatography.
:::

:::misconception
"Separating a mixture needs a chemical reaction to pull the substances
apart." No — that is compound thinking. Physical changes (boiling,
condensing, filtering, evaporating, dissolving) are enough for mixtures;
it is **compounds** that need chemical reactions such as electrolysis to
break them up.
:::

:::exam-hint
"State which separation method you would use to …" (1 mark each): pick the
method from the *mixture type*, not from habit. Mark schemes award the
method name only — "filtration", "crystallisation", "simple distillation",
"fractional distillation", "paper chromatography" — so spell out the full
name; "distillation" alone is ambiguous when fractional is intended.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join (derived-links law): spec 1.10 × 2 items — match
separation to mixture type; why forensics separates before analysis. Book
Figure 2.6 → page jump to book p. 16.
:::

sections.title: Rock salt to pure salt — filtration, crystallisation and distillation
sections.markdown:
**Filtration** separates a solid from a liquid. Pour the mixture through
filter paper: the solid left behind on the paper is the **[[residue]]**, the
liquid that comes through is the **[[filtrate]]** (Figure 2.6 — sand from
water). Filtration also separates **two solids**, provided only one of them
is soluble in water — which is exactly the trick used for rock salt below.

**Crystallisation** separates a dissolved solid (a solute) from its
solution. Heat the solution in an evaporating basin to boil off some water
until an almost **[[saturated-solution]]** solution forms — you
can test this by dipping a glass rod in and seeing if small crystals form
on its surface. Then turn the Bunsen burner off and let the crystals grow
as more water evaporates and the solution cools; filter them off at the end
(Figure 2.7).

**Rock salt** is salt contaminated with earthy, rocky impurities that are
*not* soluble in water. Crush it and mix with hot water: the salt
dissolves, the impurities do not. Filter — the insoluble impurities stay on
the filter paper as residue, and the filtrate is a clean salt solution.
Crystallise the filtrate and pure salt drops out. The same three moves
(dissolve, filter, crystallise) separate *any* pair of solids where one is
soluble and the other is not.

**Simple distillation** gets the *solvent* back instead. Boil the solution:
the water evaporates, travels into the condenser, and is condensed back to
a pure liquid to collect — while the salt stays in the flask. (Run it long
enough and the solution becomes so concentrated that the salt crystallises
out too.) One detail examiners love: water always enters the condenser at
the **lower** end, so the jacket fills completely and stays full even if
the water flow stops.

**Fractional distillation** separates two **[[miscible]]** liquids — ones
that mix in any proportion to form a single layer — using their different
boiling points: ethanol boils at 78 °C, water at 100 °C. With careful
heating the column stays at the lower temperature, so all the water
condenses inside the column and trickles back to the flask while only
ethanol vapour reaches the top and passes into the condenser. (The column
is often packed with glass beads to help the separation; the ethanol that
comes out is about 96% pure, and the last 4% of water cannot be removed by
distillation — the book files both details under "beyond International
GCSE".)

**Paper chromatography** — the technique that finishes this lesson —
separates mixtures of dyes. Most inks and food colourings are not single
colours but mixtures of dyes; chromatography splits them up the paper, and
it even works for colourless substances like sugars if a way is found to
make the spots visible. The method (spec 1.13):

- draw the **[[baseline]]** in **pencil**, about 1 cm from the bottom of the
  paper — never pen, because pen ink would move up the paper with the
  solvent;
- spot the dye mixture on the line and let it dry;
- stand the paper in a beaker with a small amount of solvent, **below the
  pencil line** — or the inks would simply dissolve into the solvent;
- put a lid (a watch glass) on the beaker so the atmosphere saturates with
  solvent vapour, which stops the solvent evaporating off the paper;
- when the solvent has risen to about 1 cm from the top, mark the highest
  level it reached — the **[[solvent-front]]** — then leave the paper to dry.

The pattern left on the paper is the **chromatogram**; reading it is §s10.

:::safety
Avoid skin contact with the solvents and the dyes, especially if you have
sensitive skin. (Book safety note for the chromatography work.)
:::

:::key-point
Water feeds into the condenser at the **lower** end: the jacket fills
better, and if the flow stops the condenser stays full of water.
:::

:::key-point
If a dye does not move from the pencil line, it is not soluble in that
solvent — try another. If it moves with the solvent front, it is *too*
soluble — try another. Finding the right solvent is done by experimenting.
:::

:::worked-example
The rock-salt run is the exam's favourite separation story, so rehearse it
as a chain: **crush + hot water** (salt dissolves, rock does not) →
**filter** (residue: insoluble impurities; filtrate: salt solution) →
**crystallise** (heat to near-saturation, rod test, Bunsen off, cool,
filter the crystals). Each arrow is a mark: method + what it removes.
:::

:::misconception
"You can get salt back from salt water by filtering the solution." No —
filtration only catches solids that are *insoluble*. Dissolved salt passes
straight through filter paper with the water; recovering it needs
crystallisation (or simple distillation, which collects the water instead).
:::

:::exam-hint
Method-choice questions follow the mixture type: insoluble solid + liquid →
**filtration**; dissolved solid from solution → **crystallisation** (want
the solid) or **simple distillation** (want the solvent); two miscible
liquids → **fractional distillation**; two solids, one soluble → **dissolve
and filter**. Describing the rock-salt method earns marks in order —
crush/dissolve, filter, crystallise — so narrate it stepwise, naming
residue and filtrate.
:::

sections.title: Using paper chromatography in analysis — Rf values
sections.markdown:
Chromatography does more than split a mixture — it tells you **what is in
it**. Suppose your unknown mixture (m) might contain dyes d1, d2, d3 and
d4. Draw a pencil line on a larger sheet, spot the mixture at one mark and
small spots of the four *known* dyes at the others, then develop the
[[chromatogram]] as in §s09 (Figure 2.13). Then compare — and measure
carefully: always measure to the **centre of the spot**.

The comparison rule: if a spot in the mixture has the **same colour** and
travelled the **same distance** as a known dye, they match. In the book's
experiment, mixture m produced spots corresponding to d1, d3 and d4. Dye
d2 is the trap: its colour matches a spot in the mixture, but it travelled
a *different* distance — so it must be a different compound.

Raw distances are unreliable, because each run's solvent moves a different
distance up the paper. So we report a ratio instead — the
**[[rf-value]]**:

> Rf = distance moved by the spot (from the pencil line) ÷ distance moved
> by the solvent front (from the pencil line)

In Figure 2.13 the solvent front moved 3.6 cm, so for dye d3: Rf =
2.9 ÷ 3.6 = **0.81**. The mixture's three spots give blue 0.9 ÷ 3.6 =
0.25, orange 2.0 ÷ 3.6 = 0.56, green 2.9 ÷ 3.6 = 0.81 — and the known dyes
give d1 = 0.56, d2 = 0.36, d3 = 0.81, d4 = 0.25. Matching values identify
the mixture's contents: **d1, d3 and d4**.

Two honesty rules about Rf: it must fall **between 0 and 1** (a value
bigger than 1 means you divided the wrong way round), and it has **no
units**. And Rf values only compare fairly on the **same paper and same
solvent** — here every spot shared one sheet, so the comparison was safe;
separate sheets are fine too, as long as paper type and solvent match.

The book's chapter questions for this section (pp. 22–23 — including the
anonymous-letter ink problem) stay in the book; this lesson's practice is
wired to the question bank below.

:::key-point
Rf value = distance moved by spot ÷ distance moved by solvent front,
measured to the centre of each spot. Rf always lies between **0 and 1**,
has **no units**, and only compares fairly on the same paper with the same
solvent.
:::

:::worked-example
Mixture m vs dyes d1–d4 (Figure 2.13, solvent front 3.6 cm): m's spots —
blue 0.25, orange 0.56, green 0.81. Known dyes — d1 0.56, d2 0.36,
d3 0.81, d4 0.25. Match: 0.25 = d4, 0.56 = d1, 0.81 = d3 → **m contains
d1, d3 and d4**. d2's colour matches but its Rf (0.36) appears nowhere in
m, so d2 is absent — colour alone never decides; distance (Rf) does.
:::

:::maths-skills
Rf is a ratio of two lengths, so the skill is division with sense-checking:
spot distance (smaller) on top, solvent-front distance (larger) below.
Sanity-check the answer — if Rf > 1 you inverted the fraction. Quote Rf to
2 decimal places, exactly as the book does (0.25, 0.56, 0.81).
:::

:::cross-curricular
**Maths:** an Rf value is a scale-invariant ratio — the same idea as a
scale factor on a map, which is exactly why it works when raw distances
change between runs.
**Forensics:** the book's anonymous-letter problem is real forensic
practice — comparing an unknown ink against a library of known inks by
matching Rf values on the same chromatogram.
:::

:::misconception
"The dye that moved furthest up the paper is simply 'the best' dye — and a
spot can travel further than the solvent." No — a spot can never overtake
the solvent front, so Rf can never exceed 1. And distance moved is not a
property to quote: Rf (on the same paper and solvent) is, because raw
distances change from run to run.
:::

:::exam-hint
Chromatogram questions have three stock mark lines: (1) same dye ⇔ same
colour **and** same distance/Rf; (2) a "minimum of N dyes" answer — count
the spots, but note two dyes could coincide in one spot (re-run with a
different solvent to check); (3) always measure to the **centre of the
spot**. And keep Rf unitless — writing "0.81 cm" throws the mark away.
:::

:::summary
- Every substance is an [[element]], a [[compound]] or a [[mixture]];
  diagrams show it: one atom type (element), two or more atom types
  **bonded in fixed proportions** (compound), different substances not
  chemically joined in **any proportion** (mixture).
- Mixtures keep their components' properties (iron stays grey, sulfur
  yellow) and separate by **physical means**; compounds have their own new
  properties and need **chemical reactions** (e.g. electrolysis) to undo.
- A pure substance melts and boils at **fixed temperatures**; a mixture
  melts and boils over a **range** — impurities lower the melting point
  and raise the boiling point.
- Separation methods: **filtration** (insoluble solid; residue vs
  filtrate), **crystallisation** (dissolved solid; evaporate to near
  saturation, cool), **simple distillation** (collect the solvent;
  condenser water enters at the bottom), **fractional distillation**
  (miscible liquids by boiling point: ethanol 78 °C vs water 100 °C).
- **Paper chromatography**: pencil baseline, solvent below the line, lid
  on, mark the solvent front; a [[chromatogram]] identifies dyes by
  matching spots; **Rf = spot distance ÷ solvent-front distance**, always
  0–1, no units, same paper and solvent to compare.
:::

- [ ] use melting-point data to decide which sample is pure?
- [ ] describe filtration, crystallisation, simple distillation and

- [ ] carry out paper chromatography correctly (pencil line, solvent below

- [ ] calculate an Rf value and use Rf matching to identify the dyes in a
      mixture?
:::
